newsitem.title: USA: US mayors offer advice to Capitol Hill on D.C..
newsitem.headline: US mayors offer advice to Capitol Hill on D.C..

text.p: Mayors from five U.S. cities on Tuesday told four House and Senate panels that oversee the financially struggling District of Columbia how their towns have overcome or averted financial calamity.

Mayors from Charlotte, N.C.; Philadelphia; Greenville, S.C.; Indianapolis, Ind.; and San Diego, Calif. offered advice at a joint hearing of D.C. subpanels of the House and Senate Appropriations Committees, the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, and the House Government Reform Committee.
"In many ways the District of Columbia is unique and cannot be compared or contrasted to any other city, U.S. Rep. Thomas Davis, R-Va., chair of the House Government Reform subpanel on D.C., said.

"But in many other important ways, its problems are familiar to all urban residents and officials," said Davis, whose panel in 1995 helped create the five-member financial control board that oversees troubled District finances.
Philadelphia Mayor Edward Rendell told the panel that a fiscal oversight board created by his state helped the city tackle a $200 million annual deficit and a "junk" bond rating in 1992.

He said Philadelphia tightened its belt rather than implement tax hikes, across-the-board service cuts and massive layoffs. "(We) squeezed every nickle of waste from the operation of City government," he said.

Rendell said the city improved tax collection, renegotiated real estate leases, cut skyrocketing employee health benefit costs, cut the number of municipal holidays, privatized some city services, and took other steps.
"Today we are reaping the benefits," he said, noting that wage and business taxes are down for the first time in 50 years and a steady exodus of businesses and jobs has ended.
Rendell said the city still faces "enormously difficult" challenges. "But the financial crisis that threatened to destroy Philadelphia's future has been resolved."
Greenville, S.C. Mayor Knox White said his town is in the midst of a 20-year journey from "bust to boom."

He said Greenville "reinvented" itself through a campaign to attract to the area not only U.S. companies, but firms from 18 foreign countries, including Germany, Japan, China, France, Holland and Belgium.

Charlotte, N.C. Mayor Patrick McCrory said his town is thriving for a variety of reasons, including its decision to appoint a full-time city manager to run the town, to contract out roughly $180 million in services to the private sector, and to set up a system of "precise costing" of city services.
"We know what it costs to (collect) garbage per house hold, to change a traffic signal bulb, and to respond to a fire emergency," said McCrory.

He said Charlotte, like D.C., has a mayor and city council. But they are part-time and they hand over day-to-day operation of the city to an appointed city manager. He urged the city to consider such a structure.
